label: thm-BM-intro
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-BM-intro}
		There are integers $\mu_\sigma(\bar\rho)\geq0$,
		depending only on $\bar\rho$ and $\sigma$, such that for any $p$-adic Hodge type $(\mathbf{w},\tau,\psi)$, the following holds
		\[
		e\bigl(R/\varpi\bigr)
		=
		\sum_{\sigma\in W(\bar\rho)}
		[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{cr},\operatorname{ss}}:\sigma]\,
		\mu_\sigma(\bar\rho),
		\]
		where $[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{cr},\operatorname{ss}}:\sigma]$ is the multiplicity of $\sigma$ occurring in the semisimplification of the mod-$\varpi$ reduction of $\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{cr}}$.
head: environment
name: Breuil--M\'ezard conjecture

label: question-1
title: Question
body_md:
\label{question-1}
		For a minimal prime $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(R)$, what is the
		Breuil--M\'ezard multiplicity
		$
		e\bigl(R/(\mathfrak{p},\varpi)\bigr)
		$
		of the corresponding irreducible component?
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
We call $\bar\rho$
		\emph{reducible and very generic} if
		\[
		\bar\rho\simeq
		\begin{pmatrix}
			\mathrm{unr}(\bar\beta_1)\omega^{a+b+1}&*\\
			0&\mathrm{unr}(\bar\beta_2)\omega^b
		\end{pmatrix},
		\qquad
		2\leq a\leq p-5,\quad 0\leq b\leq p-2,
		\]
		where $\bar\beta_1,\bar\beta_2\in\mathbb{F}^\times$.
		We call $\tau$ \emph{wildly ramified} if the least integer
		$m\geq1$ such that $\theta_1\theta_2^{-1}$ factors through
		$(\mathbb{Z}/p^m\mathbb{Z})^\times$ satisfies $m\geq2$.
head: environment

label: thm-Main-results
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-Main-results}
		Assume that $p\geq11$.
		Let $\bar\rho$ be reducible and very generic, and let
		$(\mathbf{w},\tau,\psi)$ be a $p$-adic Hodge type such that $\tau$
		is a wildly ramified principal series type.
		Put
		$R=R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi,\operatorname{cr}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$.
		For every $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(R)$, write $R(\mathfrak{p}):=R/\mathfrak{p}$.
		Then
		\[
		e(R(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)=
		\begin{cases}
			1,&\text{if $\bar\rho$ is non-split},\\
			1\text{ or }2,&\text{if $\bar\rho$ is split}.
		\end{cases}
		\]
		Moreover, if $\bar\rho$ is split, then
		$e(R(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)=1$ (resp.\ $2$) if and only if some (equivalently, every)
		closed point of $\operatorname{Spec} R(\mathfrak{p})[1/\varpi]$ corresponds
		to a reducible (resp. an irreducible) Galois representation.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
			\item By Lemma~\ref{lem comm alg2}, whenever $e(R(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)=1$,
			the ring $R(\mathfrak{p})$ is simply a formal power series ring over $\mathcal{O}$. However, our method still cannot determine how these components intersect in $R$.
			\item 
			We also determine the number of irreducible components
			of $R$.
			If $\bar\rho$ is non-split, then
			$
			\#\operatorname{Min}(R)=e(R/\varpi)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm-BM=1-non-split}).
			If $\bar\rho$ is split, then
			$
			2\#\operatorname{Min}(R)-e(R/\varpi)\in\{0,1,2\}$; see
			Corollary~\ref{cor-split-compare-mult} and
			Theorem~\ref{thm-main-thm-split} for explicit formulas.
					\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
We emphasize that Theorem~\ref{thm-Main-results} imposes no further restriction
			on the Hodge--Tate weights $k_1<k_2$. The assumptions on $\bar\rho$ and the condition $p\geq11$ are inherited from \cite{Lghost2}, as we use the main results of loc. cit to study the crystabelline slopes. 
			According to \cite{Lghost2}, the behavior of crystabelline slopes
			for a principal series type $\tau$ is \emph{much easier} to analyze
			in the wildly ramified case than in the tamely ramified case;
			see Remarks~\ref{rmk-2} and~\ref{rmk-7} for further discussion.
			There is ongoing work dealing with general principal series types $\tau$ under the same assumptions on $p$ and $\bar\rho$.
head: environment

label: cor-BM-cycles-intro
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-BM-cycles-intro}
		Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm-Main-results},
		for every $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(R)$ we have
		\[
		Z\bigl(R/(\mathfrak{p},\varpi)\bigr)
		=
		n_\sigma(\mathfrak{p})\,C(\sigma)
		+	n_{\sigma^{\operatorname{co}}}(\mathfrak{p})\,C(\sigma^{\operatorname{co}}),\quad n_\sigma(\mathfrak{p}), n_{\sigma^{\operatorname{co}}}(\mathfrak{p})\in\{0,1\}.
		\]
		Thus each Breuil--M\'ezard cycle occurs in the special
		fiber of each irreducible component of $R$ at most once.
head: environment

label: rmk-0
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk-0}
		The corresponding results also hold for unframed
		deformation rings in the non-split case and for versal
		deformation rings in the split case.
		Indeed, the framed deformation rings are formally smooth
		over the corresponding unframed or versal rings.
		This passage induces a bijection on irreducible
		components and preserves their Breuil--M\'ezard
		multiplicities; see
		\S~\ref{subsection-versal-deformation-ring}
		and Lemma~\ref{lem-1}.
head: environment

label: prop-mult=mult-intro
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-mult=mult-intro}
		The number of distinct slopes occurring in $\mathcal{X}$ is finite.
		Let $e'(\mathcal{X})$ denote this number.
		Then $e'(\mathcal{X})=e(R/\varpi)$ if $\bar\rho$ is non-split, and
		$2e'(\mathcal{X})-e(R/\varpi)\in\{0,1,2\}$ if $\bar\rho$ is split
		(see Corollary~\ref{cor-split-compare-mult} for explicit formulas).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
A feature of our approach is that we distinguish the
		irreducible components of $R$ by the crystabelline slopes
		on their generic fibers.
		More precisely, for each $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(R)$, there is a
		well-defined slope $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{p})$ such that all closed
		points of $\operatorname{Spf}(R/\mathfrak{p})^{\mathrm{rig}}$ have crystabelline slope
		$\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{p})$; see Remark~\ref{rmk-1} for further discussion.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-split-intro}

		\operatorname{Min}(A_0)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Min}(A_i)$
		sending $\mathfrak{p}$ to its preimage
		$\tilde\mathfrak{p}$ under the map in \eqref{eq-03}.

		$
		e\bigl(A_0/(\mathfrak{p},\varpi)\bigr)\leq2$

label: thm-BM
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-BM}
		For $(\mathbf{w},\tau,\psi)$ and $\bar\rho$ as above, there are integers
		$\mu_{\sigma}(\bar\rho)\geq0$, independent of $(\mathbf{w},\tau,\psi)$, such that
		\[
		e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)
		=\sum_{\sigma\in W(\bar\rho)}
		[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{ss}}:\sigma]
		\cdot\mu_{\sigma}(\bar\rho).
		\]
head: environment

label: lem-inequality-of-mult
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-inequality-of-mult}
		With the notation above, we have
		\[
		e(R/\varpi)
		=\sum_{i=1}^n e\bigl(R/(\mathfrak{p}_i+\varpi R)\bigr)
		\geq \#(\textrm{irreducible components of }R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)).
		\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The rings $R/\mathfrak{p}_i$ are $\mathcal{O}$-flat and have the same dimension as $R$.
		The equality then follows from the product decomposition of
		$R[1/\varpi]$ and Lemma~\ref{lem multiplicity-components}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $A$ be
		$R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$ or $R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\mathfrak{p}$ for some minimal prime
		ideal $\mathfrak{p}$. The \emph{Breuil--M\'ezard multiplicity} of $A$ is defined to be the
		Hilbert--Samuel multiplicity $e(A/\varpi)$ of the special fiber $A/\varpi$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Even if every irreducible component is a formal power series ring over
		$\mathcal{O}$, this does not determine the integral structure of $R$ itself.
		See \cite[Example~5.1.4]{BM02} for an illustration of this point.
head: environment

label: def-types-and-rho
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def-types-and-rho}
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item A \emph{principal series type} is a direct sum
			$\tau=\theta_1\oplus\theta_2$, where
			$\theta_i:\mathbb{Z}_p^{\times}\rightarrow E^{\times}$ are finite order characters, viewed as characters of $\operatorname{I}_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ via local class field
			theory. If $\theta_1\neq\theta_2$, its $p$-conductor is the least integer
			$m\geq1$ such that $\theta_1\theta_2^{-1}$ factors through
			$(\mathbb{Z}_p/p^m\mathbb{Z}_p)^{\times}$. If $\theta_1=\theta_2=\theta$, we set
			$m=0$. We call $\tau$ \emph{wildly ramified} if $m\geq2$.
			
			\item A reducible representation $\bar\rho$ of $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ is called
			\emph{generic} if
			\[
			\bar\rho\simeq
			\begin{pmatrix}
				\mathrm{unr}(\bar\beta_1)\omega^{a+b+1}&*\\
				0&\mathrm{unr}(\bar\beta_2)\omega^b
			\end{pmatrix},
			\]
			where $a\in\{1,\dots,p-4\}$, $b\in\{0,\dots,p-2\}$, and
			$\bar\beta_1,\bar\beta_2\in\mathbb{F}^{\times}$.
			It is called \emph{very generic} if $2\leq a\leq p-5$.
		\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: lem-type-Serre-wt
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-type-Serre-wt}
		Let $\tau$ be a principal series type, and let $\bar\rho$ be a reducible
		generic Galois representation as in Definition~\ref{def-types-and-rho}.
		Then the following statements hold.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item For $m\geq1$, denote by $\theta_1\otimes\theta_2$ the character of $\mathrm{Iw}_m$, which sends $g=(g_{i,j})_{1\leq i,j\leq2}$ to $\theta_2(\det g)(\theta_1\theta_2^{-1})(g_{11})$.
			We have
			\[
			\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)=
			\begin{cases}
				(\operatorname{Sym}^{k_2-k_1-1}E^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{-k_2})
				\otimes(\theta\circ\det),&\text{if }m=0,\\[4pt]
				(\operatorname{Sym}^{k_2-k_1-1}E^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{-k_2})
				\otimes\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{Iw}_m}^K(\theta_1\otimes\theta_2),
				&\text{if }m\geq1.
			\end{cases}
			\]
			
			\item Put
			$
			\sigma:=\operatorname{Sym}^a\mathbb{F}^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^b$, and
			$\sigma^{\mathrm{co}}:=\operatorname{Sym}^{p-3-a}\mathbb{F}^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{a+b+1}$.
			Then we have
			\[
			W(\bar\rho)=
			\begin{cases}
				\{\sigma\},&\text{if }\bar\rho\text{ is non-split},\\[4pt]
				\{\sigma,\sigma^{\mathrm{co}}\},&\text{if }\bar\rho\text{ is split}.
			\end{cases}
			\]
			
			\item The Breuil--M\'ezard multiplicity is
			\[
			e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)=
			\begin{cases}
				[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{ss}}:\sigma],
				&\text{if }\bar\rho\text{ is non-split},\\[4pt]
				[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{ss}}:\sigma]
				+[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{ss}}:
				\sigma^{\mathrm{co}}],
				&\text{if }\bar\rho\text{ is split}.
			\end{cases}
			\]
		\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[\S~4.2]{hu-paskunas}, $\sigma(\tau)$ is given by
		\[
		\sigma(\tau)=
		\begin{cases}
			\theta\circ\det,&\text{if }m=0,\\[4pt]
			\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{Iw}_m}^K(\theta_1\otimes\theta_2),&\text{if }m\geq1.
		\end{cases}
		\]
		Then (1) follows from \cite[\S~3.1]{EG1}, and (2)
		follows from \cite[\S~3.3]{EG1}.
		For each $\sigma'\in W(\bar\rho)$ in (2), $\mu_{\sigma'}(\bar\rho)=1$ by
		\cite[Proposition~1.1.3(2)]{EG1}, and hence (3) follows from Theorem~\ref{thm-BM}.
head: environment

label: prop-halo-mult
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-halo-mult}
		Keep the notation of Definition~\ref{def-types-and-rho} and
		Lemma~\ref{lem-type-Serre-wt}. Write
		$k=k_2-k_1+1$ and $\bar\theta_i|_{\Delta}=\omega^{n_i}$ for $i=1,2$.
		Consider the following integer
		\[
		s=s(\mathbf{w},\tau,\sigma):=\{k_2-(n_1-b)\}\in\{0,\dots,p-2\}.
		\]
		Assume that $m\geq1$. Then we have
		\begin{align*}
			[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{ss}}:\sigma]
			& =2(k-1)\frac{p^{m-1}-1}{p-1}
			+\left\lfloor\frac{k-2-s}{p-1}\right\rfloor
			+\left\lfloor\frac{k-2-\{s+a\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor+2,\\
			[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\operatorname{ss}}:\sigma^{\mathrm{co}}]
			& =2(k-1)\frac{p^{m-1}-1}{p-1}
			+\left\lfloor\frac{k-2-\{s-1\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor
			+\left\lfloor\frac{k-2-\{s+a+1\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor+2.
		\end{align*}
head: environment

label: eq4
title: Proof
body_md:
Twisting by $\tilde\omega^{-b}$ replaces $\bar\rho$ by
		$\bar\rho\otimes\omega^{-b}$ and $\tau$ by
		$\tau\otimes\tilde\omega^{-b}|_{I_{\mathbb{Q}_p}}$.
		On the representation-theoretic side, this tensors both
		$\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)$ and the Serre weights by $\det^{-b}$,
		and hence preserves the multiplicities in question.
		Since this twist also preserves $s$, we may assume that $b=0$.
		The definition of $s$ and \eqref{eq3} then give
		\begin{equation}\label{eq4}
			k_2-n_1\equiv s\pmod{p-1},
			\qquad
			n_2-k_1-1\equiv s+a\pmod{p-1}.
		\end{equation}
		Using the standard $K$-invariant $\mathcal{O}$-lattice inside $\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)$ and the projection formula, we have
		\[
		\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)\simeq\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{Iw}}^{K}\pi,\quad\textrm{where}\quad\pi=\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{Iw}_m}^{\mathrm{Iw}}\left((\operatorname{Sym}^{k-2}\mathbb{F}^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{-k_2})|_{\mathrm{Iw}_m}\otimes(\bar\theta_1\otimes\bar\theta_2)|_{\mathrm{Iw}_m}\right).
		\]
		Since both $\operatorname{Sym}^{k-2}\mathbb{F}^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{-k_2}$ and $\bar\theta_1\otimes\bar\theta_2$ are $\mathrm{Iw}$-representations, the projection formula gives
		$
		\pi\simeq(\operatorname{Sym}^{k-2}\mathbb{F}^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{-k_2}\otimes(\bar\theta_1\otimes\bar\theta_2))|_{\mathrm{Iw}}\otimes\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{Iw}_m}^{\mathrm{Iw}}\mathbf 1$.
		Let $\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma$ (resp. $\operatorname{Proj}_{\chi}$) be the projective envelope of $\sigma$ (resp.  a character $\chi$ of $\bar T$) in the category of profinite $\mathbb{F}[\![K]\!]$-modules (resp. $\mathbb{F}[\![\mathrm{Iw}]\!]$-modules). 
		Using the exactness of $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![K]\!]}(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma,-)$ and Frobenius reciprocity, we have
		\begin{align*}
			\bigl[\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\mathrm{ss}}:\sigma\bigr]&=\dim_\mathbb{F}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![K]\!]}(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma,\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau))=\dim_\mathbb{F}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![\mathrm{Iw}]\!]}(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma|_{\mathrm{Iw}},\pi)
			\\&=\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![\mathrm{Iw}]\!]}\left(\operatorname{Proj}_{1\times\omega^a}\oplus\operatorname{Proj}_{\omega^a\times1},\pi\right)
			=\dim_{\mathbb{F}} \left(\pi^{\bar T=1\times\omega^a}\oplus \pi^{\bar T=\omega^a\times1}\right),
		\end{align*}
		where we use $\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma|_{\mathrm{Iw}}\simeq\operatorname{Proj}_{1\times\omega^a}\oplus\operatorname{Proj}_{\omega^a\times1}$ from \cite[Lemma~6.4.1]{Pa04}. 	It remains to compute these eigenspace dimensions.
		
		Note that $\pi$ is a semisimple $\mathbb{F}[\bar T]$-module as the order of $\bar T$ is coprime to $p$.
		By Lemma~\ref{lem-rep1}, we have an isomorphism of
		$\mathbb{F}[\bar T]$-modules
		\[
		\pi\simeq
		(\operatorname{Sym}^{k_2-k_1-1}\mathbb{F}^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{-k_2})|_{\mathrm{Iw}}
		\otimes(\bar\theta_1\otimes\bar\theta_2)
		\otimes\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p-2}
		(\omega^j\otimes\omega^{p-1-j})^{\oplus m(j)}.
		\]
		We realize $\operatorname{Sym}^{k-2}\mathbb{F}^2$ as the space of homogeneous
		polynomials of degree $k-2$ in $\mathbb{F}[X,Y]$, equipped with
		the standard $K$-action.
		For $0\leq n\leq k-2$, the monomial $X^nY^{k-2-n}$,
		tensored with a vector in the $j$-th character summand
		is an eigenvector for $\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,\delta)\in\bar T$
		with eigenvalue (using \eqref{eq4})
		\[
		\alpha^{n-k_2+n_1+j}
		\delta^{k-2-n-k_2+n_2-j}
		=
		\alpha^{n-s+j}
		\delta^{\{s+a\}-n-j}.
		\]
		Hence computing the dimension of the
		$\bar T=\omega^a\times1$ eigenspace of $\pi$
		amounts to considering the solutions of the congruence
		\begin{equation}\label{eq1}
			n-s+j\equiv a\pmod{p-1},
			\qquad
			0\leq n\leq k-2,\quad 0\leq j\leq p-2.
		\end{equation}
		The other condition,
		$\{s+a\}-n-j\equiv0\pmod{p-1}$,
		is equivalent to \eqref{eq1}, since the central characters
		of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ agree.
		For each fixed $0\leq n\leq k-2$, there is a unique solution
		$j(n)\in\{0,\dots,p-2\}$ to \eqref{eq1}.
		When $j=0$, the number of solutions $0\leq n\leq k-2$
		to \eqref{eq1} is
		$
		\left\lfloor
		(k-2-\{s+a\})/(p-1)
		\right\rfloor+1$.
		Hence
		\begin{align*}
			\dim_\mathbb{F}\pi^{\bar T=\omega^a\times1}
			&=
			\#\{0\leq n\leq k-2:j(n)\neq0\}\cdot m(j)
			+\#\{0\leq n\leq k-2:j(n)=0\}\cdot m(0)\\
			&=
			(k-1)m(j\neq0)
			+\#\{0\leq n\leq k-2:j(n)=0\}\cdot
			\bigl(m(0)-m(j\neq0)\bigr)\\
			&=
			(k-1)\frac{p^{m-1}-1}{p-1}
			+\left\lfloor
			\frac{k-2-\{s+a\}}{p-1}
			\right\rfloor+1,
		\end{align*}
		where we use $m(0)=m(j\neq0)+1=C(m)+1$
		from Lemma~\ref{lem-rep1}.
		The dimensions of
		$\pi^{\bar T=1\times\omega^a}$,
		$\pi^{\bar T=\omega^{-1}\times\omega^{a+1}}$,
		and $\pi^{\bar T=\omega^{a+1}\times\omega^{-1}}$
		(the last two of which are used to compute
		$\bigl[\bar\sigma(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\mathrm{ss}}:\sigma^{\operatorname{co}}\bigr]$)
		are obtained by similar arguments.
		The proposition follows.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Retain the notation of Proposition~\ref{prop-halo-mult}, and assume
		that $b=0$. When $m\leq 1$, we relate the multiplicity
		$\bigl[\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\mathrm{ss}}:\sigma\bigr]$
		to the dimension formulas in \cite[\S~4]{Lghost}, which play a key
		role in the definition of the \emph{local ghost series} therein.
		If $m=1$, put
		\[
		d_k^{\mathrm{Iw}}
		:=
		\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![\mathrm{Iw}]\!]}
		\bigl(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma, \operatorname{Sym}^{k_2-k_1-1}\mathbb{F}^2\otimes\operatorname{det}^{-k_2}\otimes\bar\theta_1\otimes\bar\theta_2)
		=
		\bigl[\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\mathrm{ss}}:\sigma\bigr].
		\]
		This is the quantity denoted by
		$d_k^{\mathrm{Iw}}(\varepsilon\cdot(1\times\omega^{2-k}))$
		in \cite[Proposition~4.1]{Lghost}, where
		$\varepsilon=\omega^{-s}\times\omega^{s+a}$. In particular, $d_k^{\mathrm{Iw}}=\frac{2k}{p-1}+O(1)$.
		If $m=0$, so that $\theta_1=\theta_2=\theta$, put
		\[
		d_k^{\operatorname{ur}}
		:=
		\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![K]\!]}
		\bigl(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma,\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)\bigr)=	\bigl[\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\mathrm{ss}}:\sigma\bigr].
		\]
		This is the quantity denoted by $d_k^{\operatorname{ur}}(\bar\theta|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_2})$
		in \cite[(4.6.1)]{Lghost}; an explicit formula is given
		in \cite[Proposition~4.7]{Lghost}. In particular, $d_k^{\operatorname{ur}}=\frac{2k}{p^2-1}+O(1)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Keep the notation of the previous remark.
		In the case $\theta_1=\theta_2$, we may also define $d_k^{\mathrm{Iw}}$ by the same
		Hom-space formula and set $$	d_k^{\mathrm{new}}=d_k^{\mathrm{Iw}}-2d_k^{\operatorname{ur}}=\frac{2k}{p+1}+O(1),$$ which is denoted by $d_k^{\mathrm{new}}(\bar\theta|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_2})$ in \cite[Proposition~4.7]{Lghost}.
		The quantity $d_k^{\mathrm{new}}$ accounts for the contribution of
		\emph{potentially semistable but not potentially crystalline}
		representations to the
		Breuil--M\'ezard multiplicity. More precisely, for a non-split $\bar\rho$, let
		$
		R^{\operatorname{cr}}:=R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$
		be the potentially crystabelline deformation ring considered above,
		and let $R$ be the corresponding potentially semistable deformation
		ring with the same $p$-adic Hodge type.
		Write $\operatorname{St}$ for the Steinberg representation of
		$\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$ over $\mathbb{F}$, inflated to $K$.
		By the potentially semistable version of the
		Breuil--M\'ezard conjecture, we have (note that $\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{Iw}}^{K}\mathbf 1\simeq\mathbf 1\oplus\operatorname{St}$)
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			e(R/\varpi)
			&=
			\bigl[
			\bigl(\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)
			\otimes_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{St}\bigr)^{\mathrm{ss}}
			:\sigma
			\bigr]=
			\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![K]\!]}
			\bigl(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma,
			\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)
			\otimes_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{St}\bigr)\\
			&=
			\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![K]\!]}
			\bigl(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma,
			\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)
			\otimes_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{Iw}}^{K}\mathbf 1\bigr)
			-
			\dim_{\mathbb{F}}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{F}[\![K]\!]}
			\bigl(\operatorname{Proj}_\sigma,\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)\bigr)\\
			&=d_k^{\mathrm{Iw}}-d_k^{\operatorname{ur}}=d_k^{\operatorname{ur}}+d_k^{\mathrm{new}}=e(R^{\operatorname{cr}}/\varpi)+d_k^{\mathrm{new}}.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Let $R^{\mathrm{ds}}$ be the reduced quotient of $R$ defined in  \cite[\S~5]{gee-geraghty-quaternion}, which corresponds to the
		union of irreducible components on which the monodromy operator is
		generically nonzero. Then we have $d_k^{\mathrm{new}}=e(R^{\operatorname{ds}}/\varpi)$.

title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\bar T$ is abelian and has order prime to $p$, the $\mathbb{F}[\bar T]$-module $V$ admits a
		decomposition of the form \eqref{eq-lem1}.
		To determine the multiplicities $m(i)$, it suffices to restrict to
		$\Delta$, where we identify $\Delta$ with the subgroup $\operatorname{diag}(\Delta,1)$
		of $\bar T$.
		
		We claim that the action of $\Delta$ on the coset space
		$\mathrm{Iw}_m\backslash\mathrm{Iw}$ has one fixed point $\{0\}$ and
		$(p^{m-1}-1)/(p-1)$ free orbits (i.e. the stabilizer is trivial), from which we obtain
		\[
		V|_{\Delta}\cong
		\mathbf1\oplus
		\bigl(\mathbb{F}[\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}]\bigr)^{\oplus\frac{p^{m-1}-1}{p-1}},
		\qquad
		\mathbb{F}[\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}]\cong\bigoplus_{r=0}^{p-2}\omega^r.
		\]
		This gives the required values of $m(i)$.
		To prove the claim, use the coset decomposition
		\[
		\mathrm{Iw}=\bigsqcup_{t\in\mathbb{Z}_p/p^{m-1}\mathbb{Z}_p}\mathrm{Iw}_m u(t),
		\qquad
		u(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\pt&1\end{pmatrix}.
		\]
		Under this decomposition, right multiplication by
		$\operatorname{diag}([\lambda],1)$, for $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_p^{\times}$,
		sends $u(t)$ to $u([\lambda]t)$, where $[\lambda]$ denotes the Teichm\"uller
		lift of $\lambda$. Indeed,
		\[
		u(t)\begin{pmatrix}[\lambda]&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
		=\begin{pmatrix}[\lambda]&0\\pt[\lambda]&1\end{pmatrix}
		=\begin{pmatrix}[\lambda]&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}u([\lambda]t).
		\]
		Clearly, the element $t=0$ is fixed. If $\lambda\neq1$, then $[\lambda]-1$ is
		a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_p$, so no nonzero element of
		$\mathbb{Z}_p/p^{m-1}\mathbb{Z}_p$ is fixed by such $\lambda$.
		This proves the claim and the lemma.

label: def-slope-of-rep
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def-slope-of-rep}
		The \emph{(crystabelline) slope} of $\rho_x$ is defined to be the $p$-adic valuation
		\[
		\mathfrak{s}(x):=k_2-v_p(\alpha_1).
		\]
		We simply say that a slope $\mathfrak{s}$ \emph{occurs in $\mathcal{X}$} if
		$\mathfrak{s}(x)=\mathfrak{s}$ for some closed point $x\in\mathcal{X}$.
		Write
		$
		\delta_1:=x^{-k_1}(\theta_2,\alpha_2)$, and
		$
		\delta_2:=x^{-k_2}(\theta_1,\alpha_1)$.
		Then
		we have $\mathfrak{s}(x)=v_p(\delta_1(p))$.
head: environment

label: lem-crystabelline-slopes
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-crystabelline-slopes}
		Let $\rho_x$ be a crystabelline representation as above. Then $\mathfrak{s}(x)\in[0,k_2-k_1]$, and
		$\rho_x$ is reducible if and only if
		$\mathfrak{s}(x)\in\{0,k_2-k_1\}$.
head: environment

label: eq-proof1
title: Proof
body_md:
We include a proof for completeness. Weak admissibility of
		$\mathbb{D}_{\operatorname{pcrys}}(\rho_x)$ gives
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq-proof1}
			\mathfrak{s}(x)\in[0,k_2-k_1]
			\qquad\text{and}\qquad
			v_p(\alpha_1)+v_p(\alpha_2)=k_1+k_2.
		\end{equation}
		Suppose first that $\rho_x$ is reducible. If it is split, then the
		line $D_1:=E'e_1$, with its induced filtration and $(\phi,\operatorname{I}_{\mathbb{Q}_p})$-action,
		corresponds to a subrepresentation of $\rho_x$ with Hodge--Tate weight
		in $\{k_1,k_2\}$. Weak admissibility of $D_1$ therefore implies that
		$v_p(\alpha_1)\in\{k_1,k_2\}$, and hence
		$\mathfrak{s}(x)\in\{0,k_2-k_1\}$.
		If $\rho_x$ is non-split, the assertion follows from Colmez's
		classification in \cite[\S~4]{colmez-triangulline}. More precisely,
		for the trianguline parameter $s=(\delta_1,\delta_2,\infty)$ of $\rho_x$, with
		$\delta_1,\delta_2$ as in Definition~\ref{def-slope-of-rep}, we have
		\[
		\mathfrak{s}(x)=0\iff s\in\mathscr{S}_0^{\operatorname{cris}},
		\qquad
		\mathfrak{s}(x)=k_2-k_1\iff s\in\mathscr{S}_+^{\mathrm{ord}}.
		\]
		Conversely, if $\rho_x$ is irreducible, then
		its trianguline parameter $s\in\mathscr{S}_*^{\operatorname{cris}}$ by
		\cite[Proposition~4.8]{colmez-triangulline}, so
		$\mathfrak{s}(x)\in(0,k_2-k_1)$.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to construct a global analytic function
		$\alpha\in\Gamma(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}})$ whose value at each closed
		point $x$ is the Frobenius eigenvalue $\alpha_1$ on the
		$\theta_1$-isotypic line of
		$\mathbb{D}_{\operatorname{pcrys}}(\rho_x)$.
		We follow the proof of
		\cite[Proposition~7.5.3]{rozensztajn-locus}, applied to the framed
		Kisin deformation space $\mathcal{X}$.
		
		By \cite[Theorem~7.2.1]{rozensztajn-locus}, the family $\mathcal{V}$ gives
		rise to a family $\mathbb{D}_{\operatorname{pcrys}}(\mathcal{V})$ over
		$\mathcal{X}$ whose specialization at each closed point $x$ is
		$\mathbb{D}_{\operatorname{pcrys}}(\rho_x)$.
		Since $\theta_1\neq\theta_2$, applying
		\cite[Proposition~7.3.1]{rozensztajn-locus} to the inertia action
		gives a $\theta_1$-isotypic line bundle. This line bundle is preserved
		by $\phi$, since the inertia and Frobenius actions commute. Hence $\phi$ acts on this line bundle by multiplication by a
		global analytic function $\alpha$, which has the required properties.

label: cor-naive-lower-bound
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first inequality is Lemma~\ref{lem-inequality-of-mult}.
		For the second, consider the induced map of Berkovich spaces
		$
		\lambda^{\operatorname{Berk}}:\mathcal{X}^{\operatorname{Berk}}\longrightarrow\mathbb A_E^{1,\operatorname{Berk}}$.
		Consider the continuous function
		\[
		f:\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{Berk}}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,
		\qquad
		x\longmapsto k_2+\log_p|\lambda^{\operatorname{Berk}}(x)|.
		\]
		Since the subspace of classical points (i.e. $\mathcal{X}^\mathrm{cl}$) is dense in
		$\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{Berk}}$ and the image $\{f(x)=\mathfrak{s}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}^\mathrm{cl}\}$ is closed in $\mathbb R$, we deduce that $f$ is a continuous surjection from $\mathcal{X}^{\operatorname{Berk}}$ to the finite set $\{\mathfrak{s}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}^\mathrm{cl}\}$. Then $f$ is constant on each connected component of $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{Berk}}$, and thus the number of connected components of $\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{Berk}}$ (hence of $\mathcal{X}$) is at least $\#(\{\mathfrak{s}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{cl}}\})$.

label: rmk-1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{rmk-1}
		Write $R:=R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$.
		Assume that $\{\mathfrak{s}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{cl}}\}$ is finite. Then we have  the following decomposition
		\[
		\operatorname{Min}(R)=\bigsqcup_{\mathfrak{s}\in\{\mathfrak{s}(x):x\in\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{cl}}\}}\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}},\quad\textrm{where}\quad\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}=\{\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(R):\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{p})=\mathfrak{s}\}.
		\]
		Moreover, for each slope
		$\mathfrak{s}$ occurring in $\mathcal{X}$, set
		\[
		\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{s}
		:=\bigcap_{\substack{x\in\mathcal{X}^{\mathrm{cl}}\\\mathfrak{s}(x)=\mathfrak{s}}}
		(\mathfrak{m}_x\cap R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)),
		\qquad
		R_\mathfrak{s}:=R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{s},
		\]
		where $\mathfrak{m}_x$ is the maximal ideal of $R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)[1/\varpi]$ corresponding
		to $x$. Then $\mathfrak{a}_\mathfrak{s}=\cap_{\mathfrak{p}\in\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}}\mathfrak{p}$, and a closed point $x$ of
		$\operatorname{Spec} R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)[1/\varpi]$ lies in $\operatorname{Spec} R_\mathfrak{s}[1/\varpi]$ if and only if
		$\mathfrak{s}(x)=\mathfrak{s}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{cor-naive-lower-bound}, the slope is constant
		on each irreducible component of $\mathcal{X}$, which gives the asserted partition of $\operatorname{Min}(R)$. Moreover, $R[1/\varpi]$ is Jacobson by
		\cite[Lemma~15.10.5]{stack}, so each of its minimal primes

label: notation-1
title: Notation
body_md:
\label{notation-1}
		For the fixed wildly ramified type $\tau=\theta_1\oplus\theta_2$ of
		conductor $m\geq2$ and Hodge--Tate weights $k_1<k_2$, introduce the
		following notation.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item Define the character
			\[
			\varepsilon:=\bar\theta_1|_\Delta\cdot\omega^{-k_2}
			\times\bar\theta_2|_\Delta\cdot\omega^{-k_1-1}
			\]
			of $\begin{pmatrix}\Delta&0\\0&\Delta\end{pmatrix}$. We assume that $\varepsilon$ is \emph{relevant} to $\sigma=\sigma_{a,b}$, so that
			$
			\varepsilon=\omega^{-s_\varepsilon+b}\times\omega^{s_\varepsilon+a+b}$ for some
			$s_\varepsilon\in\{0,\dots,p-2\}$.
			This assumption is necessary for
			$R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$ to be nonzero. In particular, we have
			\begin{equation}
				\label{eq-1}
				\bar\theta_1|_\Delta\cdot\omega^{-k_2}=\omega^{-s_\varepsilon+b},
				\qquad
				\bar\theta_2|_\Delta\cdot\omega^{-k_1-1}=\omega^{s_\varepsilon+a+b}.
			\end{equation}
			
			\item The character $\varepsilon$ is also relevant to
			$\sigma^{\operatorname{co}}=\sigma_{p-3-a,a+b+1}$, so that $\varepsilon=\omega^{-s'_\varepsilon+b'}\times\omega^{s'_\varepsilon+a'+b'}$, where
			$
			a'=p-3-a$, $b'=a+b+1$, and $s'_\varepsilon=\{s_\varepsilon+a+1\}$.
			\item Set
			$
			w_*:=\theta_2\theta_1^{-1}(\exp(p))
			\exp\bigl(p(k_2-k_1-1)\bigr)-1\in\mathfrak{m}_{\mathbb{C}_p}$.
			Then $v_p(w_*)=1/(p^{m-2}(p-1))$.
		\end{enumerate}

title: Proposition

\label{prop-halo-slopes}

		$\operatorname{NP}(G_\sigma^{(\varepsilon)}(w_*,-))$ is

		\mathfrak{s}_n^{(\varepsilon)}\cdot v_p(w_*)

label: prop-crystabelline-slopes
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) follows from \cite[Corollary~7.8]{Lghost2}.
	We first prove (2). Write
	\[
	\bar\rho\simeq
	\begin{pmatrix}
		\mathrm{unr}(\bar\beta_1)\omega^{a+b+1}&*\neq0\\
		0&\mathrm{unr}(\bar\beta_2)\omega^b
	\end{pmatrix}
	=:\begin{pmatrix}\bar\chi_1&*\neq0\\0&\bar\chi_2\end{pmatrix}.
	\]
	For each closed point $x\in\mathcal{X}$,  $\rho_x$
	has the triangulation \eqref{eq:trangulation}, with parameters
	\[
	\delta_1=x^{-k_1}(\theta_2,\alpha_2),
	\quad\textrm{and}\quad
	\delta_2=x^{-k_2}(\theta_1,\alpha_1).
	\]
	
	If $0$ is a crystabelline slope of $\mathcal{X}$, say $\mathfrak{s}(x)=0$, then $v_p(\delta_1(p))=0$. In this case $\delta_1$ is a subrepresentation of $\rho_x$ and hence  $\bar\theta_2|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1}\equiv\bar\delta_1|_{\Delta}\equiv\omega^{a+b+1}\pmod{\varpi}$, which implies that $s_{\varepsilon}=0$ by \eqref{eq-1}. If $k_2-k_1$ is a crystabelline slope of $\mathcal{X}$, then $(\delta_1,\delta_2,\infty)\in\mathscr{S}_+^\mathrm{ord}$ as we proved in Lemma~\ref{lem-crystabelline-slopes}. Hence \cite[Proposition~4.13]{colmez-triangulline} provides another triangulation of the corresponding representation $\rho_x$, namely $(\delta_1'=(x^{-k_1})(\theta_1,\alpha_1),\delta_2'=(x^{-k_2})(\theta_2,\alpha_2),\infty)$. In this case, $v_p(\delta_1'(p))=0$ and similarly we have
	$\bar\theta_1|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1}\equiv\bar\delta'_1|_{\Delta}\equiv\omega^{a+b+1}\pmod{\varpi}$, which implies that $k_0=\{s_\varepsilon+a\}$. This proves one direction of (a) and (b).
	
	For the other direction of (2), we directly construct the required crystabelline lifts. (a) If $s_\varepsilon=0$, then consider the crystabelline characters for $i=1,2$,  $\chi_i:=\chi_{\mathrm{cycl}}^{-k_i}\cdot(\theta_{3-i},\beta_i)$, where $\beta_i\in\mathcal{O}^\times$ is a lift of $\bar\beta_i$ and $\chi_1\chi_2=\psi\chi_{\mathrm{cycl}}$ (this is possible because $(\psi\chi_{\mathrm{cycl}}^{k_1+k_2+1})|_{\operatorname{I}_{\mathbb{Q}_p}}=\theta_1\theta_2$). We first construct a closed point on $\mathcal{X}$. Note that $s_{\varepsilon}=0$ ensures that $\chi_i$ has mod-$\varpi$ reduction $\bar\chi_i$. Since $\bar\rho$ is the unique non-split extension (up to isomorphism) of $\bar\chi_2$ by $\bar\chi_1$, any non-split extension in $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}}(\chi_2,\chi_1)$ admits a $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$-invariant $\mathcal{O}$-lattice whose mod-$\varpi$ reduction is $\bar\rho$.  Note that $\theta_1\neq\theta_2$ implies that $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}}(\chi_2,\chi_1)$ is one dimensional. Moreover, each such non-split extension is indeed crystabelline, since both $\chi_i$ are crystabelline and the Hodge--Tate weight of $\chi_1\chi_2^{-1}$ is at most $-1$ (note that $\theta_1\neq\theta_2$ excludes the non-crystabelline extension). Hence we obtain a closed point $x$ of $\mathcal{X}$, and we next calculate its slope. Let $\alpha_1$ be the eigenvalue of the $\phi$-action on the subspace of $\mathbb{D}_{\operatorname{pcrys}}(\rho_x)$ where $I_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ acts through $\theta_1$. Then weak admissibility gives $v_p(\alpha_1)=k_2$, which implies that $\mathfrak{s}(x)=k_2-v_p(\alpha_1)=0$. (b) If $k_0=\{s_\varepsilon+a\}$, we take crystabelline characters $\chi_i':=\chi_{\mathrm{cycl}}^{-k_i}\cdot(\theta_{i},\beta_{i})$ with the same $\beta_i$, so that $\chi_1'\chi_2'=\psi\chi_{\mathrm{cycl}}$, and a similar argument provides a closed point $x'$ of $\mathcal{X}$ that is an extension of $\chi_2'$ by $\chi_1'$. In this case, $v_p(\alpha_1')=k_1$ and hence the slope $\mathfrak{s}(x')=k_2-v_p(\alpha'_1)=k_2-k_1$. This completes the proof of (2).
	
	We now prove (3). The ``if" part follows from (2), as for a non-split representation $\rho_x$ constructed in (2), we may choose a $G_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$-invariant $\mathcal{O}$-lattice (by conjugating $\begin{pmatrix}
		\varpi^n&0\\0&1
	\end{pmatrix}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$), such that its mod-$\varpi$ reduction is split. For the other direction, let $x$ be a closed point of $\mathcal{X}$ with slope $\mathfrak{s}(x)=0$ (resp. $k_2-k_1$). If $\rho_x$ is non-split, then $\delta_1$ (resp. $\delta_1'$) in the second paragraph is a subrepresentation of $\rho_x$; hence its mod-$\varpi$ reduction is one of $\{\bar\chi_1,\bar\chi_2\}$ (note that $\delta_1\equiv\bar\chi_i$ if and only if $\delta_2\equiv\bar\chi_{3-i}$ by comparing the determinants and a similar equivalence holds for $\delta'_i$).  Comparing the power of $\omega$ yields the required equalities in (a)(b). If $\rho_x$ is split, then $\mathbb{D}_{\operatorname{pcrys}}(\rho_x)$ is also split. Hence both $\delta_1$ (resp. $\delta'_1$) and $\delta_2$ (resp. $\delta_2'$) are subrepresentations of $\rho_x$ by checking weak admissibility. Similarly we also obtain the required equalities in this case. We complete the proof of (3).

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-BM-mult=halo-mult}Assume that $p\geq11$.
		If $\bar\rho$ is non-split, then we have
		$$
		e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)=e'\bigl(\operatorname{Spf}(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau))^{\mathrm{rig}}\bigr).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $e:=e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)$. Since the crystabelline slopes of $\mathcal{X}$ lie in $[0,k_2-k_1]$ and each slope of $\operatorname{NP}(G^{(\varepsilon)}_\sigma(w_*,-))$ has multiplicity one (Proposition~\ref{prop-halo-slopes}), our strategy is to compute the $e$th and $(e+1)$th slopes of $\operatorname{NP}(G^{(\varepsilon)}_\sigma(w_*,-))$ and compare them with $k_2-k_1$. Combining this comparison with a separate analysis of the
		boundary slopes $0$ and $k_2-k_1$, it follows from
		Proposition~\ref{prop-crystabelline-slopes} that the first $e$ slopes of $\operatorname{NP}(G^{(\varepsilon)}_\sigma(w_*,-))$ are exactly all of the slopes occurring in $\mathcal{X}$. This implies that $e=e'$.
		
		We first fix some notation. Recall that $\varepsilon=\bar\theta_1|_{\Delta}\cdot \omega^{-k_2}\times\bar\theta_2|_{\Delta}\cdot \omega^{-k_1-1}=\omega^{-s_\varepsilon+b}\times\omega^{s_\varepsilon+a+b}$, and that $w_*$ (see Notation~\ref{notation-1}) has valuation $v_p(w_*)=1/(p^{m-2}(p-1))$. Write $\bar\theta_i|_{\Delta}=\omega^{n_i}$ for $i=1,2$. Put
		\begin{itemize}
			\item 
			$e=e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)$, and $e'=e'(\operatorname{Spf}(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau))^\mathrm{rig})$.
			\item $k:=k_2-k_1+1$, $k_0=\{k-2\}$, and $k-2=k_0+k_\bullet(p-1)$.
			\item $C:=C(m,k)=(k-1)(p-1)p^{m-2}$, and $N=N(m,k)=k_\bullet+(k-1)\frac{p^{m-1}-1}{p-1}+1$.
			\item $\eta_1=\min\{s_\varepsilon,\{s_\varepsilon+a\}\}$, and $\eta_2=\max\{s_\varepsilon,\{s_\varepsilon+a\}\}$. 
		\end{itemize}
		Note that $C\cdot v_p(w_*)=k-1=k_2-k_1$.
		Since $\bar\theta_1|_\Delta\cdot\omega^{-k_2}=\omega^{-s_\varepsilon+b}$,
		Proposition~\ref{prop-halo-mult} gives
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq-pf-1}
			\begin{aligned}
				e&=\bigl[\bar{\sigma}(\mathbf{w},\tau)^{\mathrm{ss}}:\sigma\bigr]=2(k-1)\frac{p^{m-1}-1}{p-1}+\left\lfloor\frac{k-2-s_\varepsilon}{p-1}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{k-2-\{s_\varepsilon+a\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor+2
				\\&=2N+\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-s_\varepsilon}{p-1}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-\{s_\varepsilon+a\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor=2N+
				\begin{cases}
					-2& 0\leq k_0<\eta_1,\\
					-1& \eta_1\leq k_0<\eta_2,\\
					0&k_0\geq\eta_2.
				\end{cases}
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		Here the last equality follows from the formulas
		\[
		\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-s_\varepsilon}{p-1}\right\rfloor
		=
		\begin{cases}
			-1,& k_0<s_\varepsilon,\\
			0,& k_0\geq s_\varepsilon,
		\end{cases}\quad\textrm{ and }\quad
		\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-\{s_\varepsilon+a\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor
		=
		\begin{cases}
			-1,& k_0<\{s_\varepsilon+a\},\\
			0,& k_0\geq \{s_\varepsilon+a\}.

\label{rmk-2}
		The equality in Proposition~\ref{prop-BM-mult=halo-mult} relies
		on two features of our setting: $\bar\rho$ has a unique Serre
		weight, and the principal series type is wildly ramified.
		The latter condition implies that $w_*$ lies in the \emph{halo region} of
		\cite{Lghost2}, where every slope of
		$\operatorname{NP}(G_\sigma^{(\varepsilon)}(w_*,-))$ has multiplicity one.
		
		When $\bar\rho$ is split, it has two Serre weights, and the
		equality $e=e'$ no longer holds. As we will see in
		Corollary~\ref{cor-split-compare-mult}, $e$ is approximately
		twice $e'$.
		If $\tau$ is a tamely ramified principal series type, the corresponding parameter $w'_*$ lies in the central region of the weight disc. In this case, the ``near-Steinberg'' phenomenon gives rise to long segments of constant slope in $\operatorname{NP}(G^{(\varepsilon)}_\sigma(w'_*,-))$, and usually we have $e'<e$; see \cite[Proposition~2.17(5)]{Lghost2}. The relationship between $e$ and $e'$ in this case is more subtle, and we leave its investigation to future work.

label: lem-multiplicity-difference
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-multiplicity-difference}
		Let $e_1$ and $e_2$ be the multiplicities $e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)$ for the
		two non-split residual representations with Serre weight sets
		$\{\sigma_{a,b}\}$ and $\{\sigma_{p-3-a,a+b+1}\}$, respectively.
		Recall that $k_0=\{k_2-k_1-1\}$ and
		$s_\varepsilon\in\{0,\dots,p-2\}$ is defined in Notation~\ref{notation-1}.
		Set $s'_\varepsilon:=\{s_\varepsilon+a+1\}$ and $a':=p-3-a$.
		Then $e_1-e_2$ is given by the following table.
		
		\begin{center}
			\renewcommand{1.6}{1.2}
			\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2pt}
			\begin{tabular}{c|l}
				\hline
				$e_1-e_2$ & Conditions \\
				\hline
				$2$
				& $s_\varepsilon=0,\quad k_0=\{s_\varepsilon+a\}$
				\\
				\hline
				\multirow{2}{*}{$1$}
				& $s_\varepsilon=0,\quad	k_0\notin\bigl\{\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\},\{s_\varepsilon+a\}\bigr\}$
				\\
				& $s_\varepsilon\neq0,\quad s'_\varepsilon\neq 0,\quad k_0=\{s_\varepsilon+a\}$
				\\
				\hline
				\multirow{3}{*}{$0$}
				& $s_\varepsilon=0,\quad k_0=\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}$\\
				&$s'_\varepsilon=0,\quad k_0=\{s_\varepsilon+a\}$
				\\
				& $s_\varepsilon\neq0,\quad s'_\varepsilon\neq0,\quad
				k_0\notin\bigl\{\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\},\{s_\varepsilon+a\}\bigr\}$
				\\
				\hline
				\multirow{2}{*}{$-1$}
				& $s'_\varepsilon=0,\quad k_0\notin\bigl\{\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\},\{s_\varepsilon+a\}\bigr\}$
				\\
				& $s_\varepsilon\neq0,\quad s'_\varepsilon\neq 0,\quad k_0=\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}$
				\\
				\hline
				$-2$
				& $s'_\varepsilon=0,\quad k_0=\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}$
				\\
				\hline
			\end{tabular}
		\end{center}

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop-halo-mult},
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			e_1-e_2
			&=\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-s_\varepsilon}{p-1}\right\rfloor
			+\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-\{s_\varepsilon+a\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-\{s_\varepsilon+a+1\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor
			-\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-\{s_\varepsilon-1\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Note that $s'_\varepsilon=\{s_\varepsilon+a+1\}$ and
		$\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}=\{s_\varepsilon-1\}$. For $0\leq r,k_0\leq p-2$,
		\[
		\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-r}{p-1}\right\rfloor
		-\left\lfloor\frac{k_0-\{r+1\}}{p-1}\right\rfloor
		=\mathbf1_{k_0=r}-\mathbf1_{r=p-2}.
		\]
		Applying this identity with $r=\{s_\varepsilon+a\}$ and
		$r=\{s_\varepsilon-1\}$ gives the required differences.

label: cor-split-compare-mult
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-split-compare-mult}Assume that $p\geq11$.
		Retain the notation of Lemma~\ref{lem-multiplicity-difference},
		and suppose that $\bar\rho$ is split. Recall that $k=k_2-k_1+1$ and $k_0=\{k_2-k_1-1\}$. Write
		$
		\mathcal{X}:=\operatorname{Spf}(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau))^{\mathrm{rig}}$, $e:=e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)$, and $e':=e'(\mathcal{X})$.
		Then the following statements hold and cover all possible cases.
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item If $s_\varepsilon\neq0$, $s'_\varepsilon\neq0$, and
			$
			k_0\notin\bigl\{\{s_\varepsilon+a\},\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}\bigr\}$,
			then neither $0$ nor $k-1$ occurs as a crystabelline
			slope of $\mathcal{X}$, and
			$				
			e=2e'.
			$
			\item If exactly one of $s_\varepsilon,s'_\varepsilon$ is zero  and
			$
			k_0\notin\bigl\{\{s_\varepsilon+a\},\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}\bigr\},
			$
			then $0$ is the only boundary slope occurring in
			$\mathcal{X}$, and $e+1=2e'$.
			
			\item If $s_\varepsilon\neq0$, $s'_\varepsilon\neq0$, and
			$
			k_0\in\bigl\{\{s_\varepsilon+a\},\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}\bigr\}$,
			then $k-1$ is the only boundary slope occurring in
			$\mathcal{X}$, and $e+1=2e'$.
			
			\item If exactly one of $s_\varepsilon,s'_\varepsilon$ is zero and
			$
			k_0\in\bigl\{\{s_\varepsilon+a\},\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}\bigr\},
			$
			then both $0$ and $k-1$ occur as crystabelline
			slopes of $\mathcal{X}$, and
			$
			e+2=2e'$.
		\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $e_1$, $e_2$ be the Breuil--M\'ezard multiplicities defined in Lemma~\ref{lem-multiplicity-difference}, and denote by $e'_1$, $e'_2$ the corresponding naive lower bounds. From Proposition~\ref{prop-BM-mult=halo-mult} and Lemma~\ref{lem-type-Serre-wt}(3), we obtain $e_i=e'_i$ for $i=1,2$ and $e=e_1+e_2$. By Proposition~\ref{prop-crystabelline-slopes}, we have $e'=\max\{e'_1,e_2'\}$, except for $s_\varepsilon=0$ and $k_0=\{s'_{\varepsilon}+a'\}$, or $s'_\varepsilon=0$ and $k_0=\{s_{\varepsilon}+a\}$, in which cases $e'=e_1'+1=e_2'+1$.
		Now (1)(2)(3)(4) follow from Proposition~\ref{prop-crystabelline-slopes} and  Lemma~\ref{lem-multiplicity-difference}.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm-BM=1-non-split}
		Assume that $p\geq11$.
		Let $\bar\rho$ be a reducible, non-split, and very generic local representation. Let $\tau$ be a wildly ramified principal series type. Write $\operatorname{Min}(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau))=\{\mathfrak{p}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{p}_n\}$, and $R(\mathfrak{p}_i):=R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\mathfrak{p}_i$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\mathcal{X}=\operatorname{Spf}(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau))^\mathrm{rig}$.
		By Corollary~\ref{cor-naive-lower-bound}, Proposition~\ref{prop-crystabelline-slopes}, and Proposition~\ref{prop-BM-mult=halo-mult}, we have
		\[
		e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi)\geq n\geq e'(\mathcal{X})=e(R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\varpi).

label: lem-1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-1}
		Let $A$ be one of $R_1(\mathbf{w},\tau)$, $R_2(\mathbf{w},\tau)$, or
		$R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$, and let
		$A^\square=R_{\bar\rho}^{\square,\psi}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$
		be the corresponding framed Kisin ring.
		Then $A$ is a reduced, equidimensional, complete Noetherian
		local $\mathcal{O}$-flat algebra, and $A[1/\varpi]$
		is regular. Moreover,
		$
		e(A/\varpi)=e(A^\square/\varpi)$,
		and extension of ideals induces a bijection
		\begin{equation}\label{eq-pf-2}
			\operatorname{Min}(A)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Min}(A^\square):
			\qquad
			\mathfrak{p}\longmapsto\mathfrak{p} A^\square.
		\end{equation}
		For every $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(A)$, we also have
		$
		e\bigl(A/(\mathfrak{p},\varpi)\bigr)
		=
		e\bigl(A^\square/(\mathfrak{p} A^\square,\varpi)\bigr)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By construction, $A$ is a reduced complete Noetherian local
		$\mathcal{O}$-flat algebra.
		The map $A\to A^\square$ is formally smooth and induces an
		isomorphism on residue fields, hence 
		$
		A^\square\simeq A[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$.
		Consequently,
		$
		A^\square/\varpi
		\simeq (A/\varpi)[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$, and this gives
		$e(A/\varpi)=e(A^\square/\varpi)$.
		
		For every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $A$, we have
		$
		A^\square/\mathfrak{p} A^\square
		\simeq (A/\mathfrak{p})[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$.
		Thus $\mathfrak{p} A^\square$ is prime and
		$\mathfrak{p} A^\square\cap A=\mathfrak{p}$.
		If $\mathfrak{p}$ is minimal and $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak{p} A^\square$
		is a prime ideal, then $\mathfrak q\cap A=\mathfrak{p}$, which forces
		$\mathfrak{p} A^\square\subseteq\mathfrak q$.
		Hence $\mathfrak{p} A^\square$ is minimal, and
		\eqref{eq-pf-2} is well-defined and injective.
		Conversely, if $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Min}(A^\square)$, going-down
		for the flat map $A\to A^\square$
		\cite[Lemma~10.11]{eis} implies that
		$\mathfrak{p}:=\mathfrak q\cap A$ is a minimal prime of $A$.
		Since $\mathfrak{p} A^\square$ is a prime ideal contained in
		$\mathfrak q$, minimality gives
		$\mathfrak q=\mathfrak{p} A^\square$.
		This proves the bijection.
		
		By Theorem~\ref{thm-Kisin}, $A^\square$ is equidimensional.
		For every $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(A)$, the preceding bijection gives
		$
		\dim(A/\mathfrak{p})
		=
		\dim(A^\square/\mathfrak{p} A^\square)-n
		=
		\dim A^\square-n
		=
		\dim A$.
		Thus $A$ is equidimensional.
		Moreover,
		$
		A^\square/(\mathfrak{p} A^\square,\varpi)
		\simeq
		\bigl(A/(\mathfrak{p},\varpi)\bigr)[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]$
		gives the asserted equality
		for the special fibers of corresponding irreducible components.
		
		Finally, $A\to A^\square$ is a flat local homomorphism,
		hence faithfully flat \cite[Lemma~10.39.17]{stack}.
		Its base change
		$
		A[1/\varpi]\longrightarrow A^\square[1/\varpi]$
		is also faithfully flat by
		\cite[Lemma~10.39.7]{stack}.
		Since $A^\square[1/\varpi]$ is regular by
		Theorem~\ref{thm-Kisin}, faithful flat descent of regularity
		\cite[Lemma~10.164.4]{stack} shows that $A[1/\varpi]$
		is regular.

\label{def-reducible-type}
		Let $x$ be a closed point of $\operatorname{Spec} R(\mathbf{w},\tau)[1/\varpi]$. If $\rho_x$ is irreducible, then we say $x$ is of \emph{reducibility type} $\operatorname{irr}$. Otherwise, we say that $x$ is of
		reducibility type $1$ (resp. $2$) if
		$
		\kappa_1\equiv\bar\chi_1\pmod{\varpi_{E'}}$ (resp. $
		\kappa_1\equiv\bar\chi_2\pmod{\varpi_{E'}}$), where $ \varpi_{E'}$ generates the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{E'}$.
		For $*\in\{1,2,\mathrm{irr}\}$, we define
		$I_*^{\mathrm{ver}}$ to be the ideal of $R^{\mathrm{ver}}$ and
		$I_*^{\mathrm{ps}}$ to be the ideal of $R^{\mathrm{ps}}$ given by
		\[
		I_*^{\mathrm{ver}}
		:=
		R^{\mathrm{ver}}\cap\bigcap_x\mathfrak{m}_x,
		\qquad
		I_*^{\mathrm{ps}}
		:=
		R^{\mathrm{ps}}\cap I_*^{\mathrm{ver}},
		\]
		where the intersection is taken over all closed points
		$
		x\in\operatorname{Spec}
		R^{\mathrm{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)[1/p]

\label{prop:kisin rings relation}

		=
		R^{\mathrm{ps}}[\![x,y]\!]/(xy-c)$, and $R^{\mathrm{ps}}\xrightarrow{\sim}R_i$ for $i=1,2$.
		Then we have $I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ver}}=I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ps}}R^{\operatorname{ver}}$, $I_1^{\operatorname{ver}}=I_1^{\operatorname{ps}}R^{\operatorname{ver}}+(x)$, and $I_2^{\operatorname{ver}}=I_2^{\operatorname{ps}}R^{\operatorname{ver}}+(y)$. Moreover, the above isomorphisms induce the following isomorphisms.
		\begin{align*}
			&R^{\mathrm{ps}}/
			\bigl(I_i^{\mathrm{ps}}\cap I_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\mathrm{ps}}\bigr)
			\cong R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau),\quad\textrm{and} \quad
			R^{\mathrm{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)\simeq R^{\operatorname{ver}}/(I^{\operatorname{ver}}_{\operatorname{irr}}\cap I^{\operatorname{ver}}_{1}\cap I^{\operatorname{ver}}_{2}).\\
			&(R^{\mathrm{ps}}/I_1^{\mathrm{ps}})[\![y]\!]
			\cong
			R^{\mathrm{ver}}/I_1^{\mathrm{ver}},
			\qquad
			(R^{\mathrm{ps}}/I_2^{\mathrm{ps}})[\![x]\!]
			\cong
			R^{\mathrm{ver}}/I_2^{\mathrm{ver}},
			\quad \textrm{and}\quad
			\frac{(R^{\mathrm{ps}}/I_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\mathrm{ps}})[\![x,y]\!]}{(xy-c)}
			\cong
			R^{\mathrm{ver}}/I_{\mathrm{irr}}^{\mathrm{ver}}.
		\end{align*}

label: rmk-4
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk-4}
		By Proposition~\ref{prop-crystabelline-slopes} and its proof, we have the following observations. A type $1$ (resp. type $2$) point occurs in $\operatorname{Spec} R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)[1/\varpi]$ if and only if 
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq-3}
			\begin{aligned}
				\omega^{a+b+1}\textrm{ (resp. }\omega^b\textrm{)}\in\{\bar\theta_1|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1},\bar\theta_2|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1}\}.
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		Moreover, the following table summarizes equivalent conditions to \eqref{eq-3}.
		In each row, the conditions in the last two columns are equivalent
		to each other and to the existence of a type $i\in\{1,2\}$ point on $\operatorname{Spec} R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)[1/\varpi]$ of slope $\mathfrak{s}\in\{0,k_2-k_1\}$,
		with the type and slope specified in the first column.
		\begin{table}[H]
			\centering
			\renewcommand{1.6}{1.4}
			\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
				\hline
				Type and slope & Character condition & Numerical condition \\
				\hline
				Type $1$, slope $k_2-k_1$
				& $\bar\theta_1|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1}=\omega^{a+b+1}$
				& $k_0=\{s_\varepsilon+a\}$ \\
				\hline
				Type $1$, slope $0$
				& $\bar\theta_2|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1}=\omega^{a+b+1}$
				& $s_\varepsilon=0$ \\
				\hline
				Type $2$, slope $k_2-k_1$
				& $\bar\theta_1|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1}=\omega^b$
				& $k_0=\{s'_\varepsilon+a'\}=\{s_\varepsilon-1\}$ \\
				\hline
				Type $2$, slope $0$
				& $\bar\theta_2|_{\Delta}\cdot\omega^{-k_1}=\omega^b$
				& $s'_\varepsilon=\{s_\varepsilon+a+1\}=0$ \\
				\hline
			\end{tabular}
		\end{table}
		Again, by our genericity assumption, for each
		$\mathfrak{s}\in\{0,k_2-k_1\}$, type $1$ and type $2$ points of
		slope $\mathfrak{s}$ cannot both occur on
		$\operatorname{Spec} R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)[1/\varpi]$.

label: lem-relation-slope-and-reducible-type
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq-5
title: Proof
body_md:
For (1), the ring $A[1/\varpi]$ is Jacobson
		by \cite[Lemma~15.10.5]{stack}, and
		Lemma~\ref{lem-crystabelline-slopes} gives
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq-5}
			\begin{aligned}
				I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ver}}
				= A\cap
				\bigcap_{\rho_x\text{ irreducible}}\mathfrak m_x 
				= A\cap
				\bigcap_{\mathfrak{p}\in\Sigma_{(0,k_2-k_1)}(\bar\rho_0)}\mathfrak{p} A[1/\varpi]
				= \bigcap_{\mathfrak{p}\in\Sigma_{(0,k_2-k_1)}(\bar\rho_0)}\mathfrak{p}.
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		Since $A$ has finitely many minimal primes, it follows that for every $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(A)$,
		$
		I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ver}}\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$ if and only if $
		\mathfrak{p}\in\Sigma_{(0,k_2-k_1)}(\bar\rho_0)$.
		For such a prime $\mathfrak{p}$, any closed point $x$ of $V(\mathfrak{p} A[1/\varpi])$ corresponds to an irreducible representation $\rho_x$, hence
		$c\notin\mathfrak m_x$. This implies that $c\notin\mathfrak{p}$.
		
		For (2), let $\mathfrak{p}\in\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}(\bar\rho_0)$, where
		$\mathfrak{s}\in\{0,k_2-k_1\}$.
		By our genericity assumption and Remark~\ref{rmk-4},
		all closed points of $\operatorname{Spec} A[1/\varpi]$ of slope $\mathfrak{s}$ have the
		same type $i$, as specified in \eqref{eq-4}.
		In particular, every closed point of $V(\mathfrak{p} A[1/\varpi])$ has type $i$ and slope $\mathfrak{s}$.
		Since $A[1/\varpi]$ is Jacobson, we obtain
		$$I^{\operatorname{ver}}_{i}=\bigcap_{x\textrm{ of type } i}(\mathfrak{m}_x\cap A)\subseteq\bigcap_{\substack{x\textrm{ of type } i\\\mathfrak{s}(x)=\mathfrak{s}}}(\mathfrak{m}_x\cap A)\subseteq\bigcap_{\substack{
				x\textrm{ of type } i\\
				\mathfrak{s}(x)=\mathfrak{s}\\
				\mathfrak{p}\subseteq\mathfrak{m}_x\cap A
		}}(\mathfrak{m}_x\cap A)=\mathfrak{p}.$$
		It remains to show that $I_{3-i}^{\operatorname{ver}}\not\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$.
		Set $\mathfrak{s}'=k_2-k_1-\mathfrak{s}$.
		As we mentioned above, no type $3-i$ point has slope
		$\mathfrak{s}$, and thus every type $3-i$ point has slope $\mathfrak{s}'$.
		Consequently,
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			I_{3-i}^{\operatorname{ver}}
			&= \bigcap_{x\text{ of type }3-i}
			(\mathfrak m_x\cap A) \supseteq
			\bigcap_{\mathfrak{s}(x)=\mathfrak{s}'}
			(\mathfrak m_x\cap A)
			= \bigcap_{\mathfrak{p}'\in\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}'}(\bar\rho_0)}\mathfrak{p}'.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Suppose that $I_{3-i}^{\operatorname{ver}}\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$. 
		If $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}'}(\bar\rho_0)$ is empty,  then $A=I_{3-i}^{\operatorname{ver}}$, and hence the preceding inclusion gives $A=I_{3-i}^{\operatorname{ver}}\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$, a contradiction.
		Otherwise,
		there is some
		$\mathfrak{p}'\in\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}'}(\bar\rho_0)$ such that $\mathfrak{p}'=\mathfrak{p}$, which is a contradiction by comparing the slopes.
		Thus $I_{3-i}^{\operatorname{ver}}\not\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$, as required.

title: Remark
body_md:
The proof of \cite[Lemma~6.4]{paskunas-2adic} shows that every
		closed point $x$ of the generic fiber whose maximal ideal contains

label: prop-key-irreducible
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-key-irreducible}
		The prime ideal $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ is minimal and hence corresponds to an irreducible component of $R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)$. In particular, $R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\tilde{\mathfrak{p}}_i$ is a formal power series ring over $\mathcal{O}$. Moreover, we have the following isomorphism
		\[
		(R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\tilde{\mathfrak{p}}_i)[\![x,y]\!]/(xy-\bar c)\simeq R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})=R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\mathfrak{p},
		\]
		where $\bar c$ is the image of $c$ in $R^{\operatorname{ps}}/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$, and  $e(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)\leq2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From \eqref{eq-pf-3}, we have the following homomorphisms
		\[
		R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)
		\simeq R^{\operatorname{ps}}/(I^{\operatorname{ps}}_{\operatorname{irr}}\cap I^{\operatorname{ps}}_i)
		\twoheadrightarrow R^{\operatorname{ps}}/I^{\operatorname{ps}}_{\operatorname{irr}}
		\longrightarrow
		\frac{(R^{\operatorname{ps}}/I^{\operatorname{ps}}_{\operatorname{irr}})[\![x,y]\!]}{(xy-c)}
		\simeq R^{\operatorname{ver}}/I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ver}}.
		\]
		By the corollary after \cite[Theorem~22.6]{mat} (see also \cite[Lemma~6.2]{paskunas-2adic}), the homomorphism $R^{\operatorname{ps}}/I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ps}}\rightarrow R^{\operatorname{ver}}/I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ver}}$ is flat (taking $A=R^{\operatorname{ps}}/I^{\operatorname{ps}}_{\operatorname{irr}}$, $B=A[\![x,y]\!]$, $f(x,y)=xy-c$). Hence going-down for a flat map (\cite[Lemma~10.11]{eis}) implies that the prime ideal $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ is minimal over $I^{\operatorname{ps}}_{\operatorname{irr}}$. Moreover, by Lemma~\ref{lem-minimal-primes}(2), $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i\notin V(I_{i}^{\operatorname{ps}})$ implies that $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ is also a minimal prime ideal over $I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ps}}\cap I_i^{\operatorname{ps}}$, and hence a minimal prime of $R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)
		\simeq R^{\operatorname{ps}}/(I^{\operatorname{ps}}_{\operatorname{irr}}\cap I^{\operatorname{ps}}_i)$.
		Therefore, we deduce that $R^{\operatorname{ps}}/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i=R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ is a formal power series ring by Theorem~\ref{thm-BM=1-non-split} and Remark~\ref{rmk-3}.
		Next,  consider the following homomorphisms obtained by reducing modulo $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$
		\[
		C:=\frac{(R^{\operatorname{ps}}/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i)[[x,y]]}{(xy-\bar c)}
		\simeq
		\frac{R^{\operatorname{ps}}[[x,y]]/(xy-c)}
		{\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i\bigl(R^{\operatorname{ps}}[[x,y]]/(xy-c)\bigr)}= \frac{R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)}{\tilde\mathfrak{p}_iR^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)}
		\twoheadrightarrow R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\mathfrak{p}.
		\]
		Since $c\notin\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$, we have that $C$ is an integral domain, which implies that $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$ is a prime ideal. This forces $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$ to be an equality, since $\mathfrak{p}$ is a minimal prime ideal of $R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$. Hence we obtain the required isomorphism. The last inequality $e(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)\leq2$ then follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:mult leq 2}.

label: prop-key-reducible
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-key-reducible}
		The prime ideal $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ is minimal and hence corresponds to an irreducible component of $R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)$. In particular, $R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\tilde{\mathfrak{p}}_i$ is a formal power series ring over $\mathcal{O}$. Moreover, we have the following isomorphism
		\[
		(R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\tilde{\mathfrak{p}}_i)[\![z_i]\!]\simeq R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})=R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\mathfrak{p}.
		\]
		In particular, $R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})$ is a formal power series ring and $e(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is similar to that of
		Proposition~\ref{prop-key-irreducible}.
		Using the flatness of the map
		$
		R^{\operatorname{ps}}/I_i^{\operatorname{ps}}
		\rightarrow
		(R^{\operatorname{ps}}/I_i^{\operatorname{ps}})[\![z_i]\!]
		$
		and going-down, we deduce that $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i/I_i^{\operatorname{ps}}$ is a
		minimal prime of $R^{\operatorname{ps}}/I_i^{\operatorname{ps}}$.
		Moreover,
		$\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i\in V(I_i^{\operatorname{ps}})\setminus V(I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ps}})$,
		together with Lemma~\ref{lem-minimal-primes}(2), implies
		that  $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ is a minimal prime ideal of
		$
		R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)\simeq
		R^{\operatorname{ps}}/(I_i^{\operatorname{ps}}\cap I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ps}})
		$. Hence
		$
		R^{\operatorname{ps}}/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i
		\simeq R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i
		$
		is a formal power series ring over $\mathcal{O}$ by
		Theorem~\ref{thm-BM=1-non-split} and
		Remark~\ref{rmk-3}.
		Next, reducing modulo $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ gives
		\[
		C:=(R^{\operatorname{ps}}/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i)[\![z_i]\!]
		\simeq
		\frac{R^{\operatorname{ver}}/I_i^{\operatorname{ver}}}
		{\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i(R^{\operatorname{ver}}/I_i^{\operatorname{ver}})}
		\simeq
		\frac{R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)}{\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)+(z_{3-i})}
		\twoheadrightarrow R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\mathfrak{p}.
		\]
		Here the second isomorphism follows from the relations $I_i^{\operatorname{ver}}=I_i^{\operatorname{ps}}R^{\operatorname{ver}}+(z_{3-i})$ and $
		I_i^{\operatorname{ps}}\subseteq\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$, and the last map follows from
		$\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$ and $z_{3-i}\in\mathfrak{p}$.
		Since $C$ is an integral domain, indeed a formal power
		series ring over $\mathcal{O}$, the ideal
		$\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)+(z_{3-i})$ is prime.
		The minimality of $\mathfrak{p}$ therefore gives
		$
		\mathfrak{p}=\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)+(z_{3-i})$.
		This proves the required isomorphism.
		In particular, $R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})$ is a formal power series
		ring over $\mathcal{O}$, and
		$e(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)=1$.

title: Proof
body_md: This follows directly from Proposition~\ref{prop-key-reducible}, and the map is given by $\mathfrak{p}\mapsto\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$, where $i\in\{1,2\}$ is determined by $\mathfrak{p}$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem-relation-slope-and-reducible-type}(2). This map is injective because $\mathfrak{p}=\tilde\mathfrak{p}_iR^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)+(z_{3-i})$. Note that the image of $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}(\bar\rho_0)$ lies in $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}(\bar\rho_1)\sqcup\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}(\bar\rho_2)$ for $\mathfrak{s}\in\{0,k_2-k_1\}$ and at most one of $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}(\bar\rho_1)$ and $\Sigma_{\mathfrak{s}}(\bar\rho_2)$ is non-empty by our genericity assumption.

label: rmk-5
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk-5}
		By \cite[Theorem~7.3]{paskunas-2adic} (together with the geometric Breuil--M\'ezard conjecture for non-split $\bar\rho_1$ and $\bar\rho_2$), the \emph{special fiber} of
		$R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)$ is contained in the reducible locus. This gives
		a direct proof that
		$
		e(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)=2$ for $\mathfrak{p}\in\Sigma_{(0,k_2-k_1)}(\bar\rho_0)$.
		Indeed, let $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ be a corresponding minimal prime in Proposition~\ref{prop-key-irreducible}. The image of $c$ in
		$R^{\operatorname{ps}}/(I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ps}},\varpi)$ is nilpotent. Since
		$I_{\operatorname{irr}}^{\operatorname{ps}}\subseteq\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$, its image in
		$
		R^{\operatorname{ps}}/(\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i,\varpi)
		\simeq R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/(\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i,\varpi)$
		is also nilpotent. As $R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ is a formal power
		series ring over $\mathcal{O}$, the image of $c$ in this special fiber is zero.
		Proposition~\ref{prop-key-irreducible} therefore gives
		\[
		R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi
		\simeq
		\mathbb{F}[\![T_1,\dots,T_n,x,y]\!]/(xy),
		\qquad
		n=\dim(R^{\operatorname{ps}}/\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i)-1.
		\]
		Consequently, this \emph{special fiber} has multiplicity $2$ and
		exactly two irreducible components.

label: rmk-6
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk-6}
		Let $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Min}(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau))$, and let $\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i$ denote
		the corresponding minimal prime of $R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)$ for each relevant $i$,
		as provided by Propositions~\ref{prop-key-irreducible} and
		\ref{prop-key-reducible}. Then
		$
		e(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi)
		=
		\sum_i e\bigl(R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/(\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i,\varpi)\bigr)$,
		where the sum runs over both $i=1,2$ if
		$\mathfrak{p}\in\Sigma_{(0,k_2-k_1)}(\bar\rho_0)$, and over the single
		index $i\in\{1,2\}$ specified in \eqref{eq-4} otherwise.
		We may upgrade this equality to an equality of cycles via results in \cite[\S~7]{paskunas-2adic}.
		More precisely, put $d=\dim R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathbf{w},\tau)$, and recall 
		the cycle map defined in
		\cite[\S~7, Equation~(15)]{paskunas-2adic}
		$$\alpha:\mathscr{Z}_{d-2}(R_1/(c))\oplus\mathscr{Z}_{d-2}(R_2/(c))\hookrightarrow\mathscr{Z}_{d-1}(R^{\operatorname{ver}}/(c)),$$
		where $\mathscr{Z}_{\ell}(A)$ is the group of $\ell$-dimensional cycles of a Noetherian ring $A$. Write $\alpha_1(Z):=\alpha(Z,0)$ and $\alpha_2(Z):=\alpha(0,Z)$ for the restrictions to the two summands.	
		Applying the
		argument of \cite[Theorem~7.1]{paskunas-2adic} to each irreducible component gives
		\[
		z_{d-1}\bigl(R^{\operatorname{ver}}(\mathfrak{p})/\varpi\bigr)
		=
		\sum_i
		\alpha_i\!\left(
		z_{d-2}\bigl(R_i(\mathbf{w},\tau)/(\tilde\mathfrak{p}_i,\varpi)\bigr)
		\right),
		\]
		where $z_\ell(R)$ denotes the $\ell$-dimensional cycle associated to $R$.

label: lem-ca1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-ca1}
		Let $a\in\mathfrak{m}$ be a non-zero-divisor, and set
		$
		\mathrm{ord}_{\mathfrak{m}}(a):=\max\{j\geq 0:a\in\mathfrak{m}^j\}$.
		Then we have
		$
		e(A/a)\geq \mathrm{ord}_{\mathfrak{m}}(a)\cdot e(A)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $a\in\mathfrak{m}$ is a non-zero-divisor,
		$\dim(A/a)=\dim A-1$, so $a$ is part of a system of parameters
		of $A$; see, for example,
		\cite[Lemma~10.60.13]{stack} and its proof.
		The assertion then follows from \cite[Theorem~14.9]{mat}.
head: environment

label: lem:mult leq 2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mult leq 2}
		Let
		$
		A:=
		\frac{\mathbb{F}[\![T_1,\dots,T_n]\!][\![x,y]\!]}{(xy-c)}$,
		where $c\in(T_1,\dots,T_n)$.
		Write
		$
		\mathrm{ord}(c):=
		\max\{j\geq 0:c\in(T_1,\dots,T_n)^j\}
		$.
		Then we have
		$
		e(A)=\min\{2,\mathrm{ord}(c)\}\leq 2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $S=\mathbb{F}[\![x,y,T_1,\dots,T_n]\!]$,
		$f=xy-c$, and $\mathfrak{m}=(x,y,T_1,\dots,T_n)\subseteq S$.
		Since $S$ is a regular local ring and $f\neq 0$,
		\cite[(40.2)]{Nagata} gives
		$
		e(A)=\mathrm{ord}_{\mathfrak{m}}(f)$.
		As $c$ involves only $T_1,\dots,T_n$, we have
		$
		\mathrm{ord}_{\mathfrak{m}}(f)=\min\{2,\mathrm{ord}(c)\}$,
		which proves the assertion.

label: lem comm alg2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem comm alg2}
		Let $A$ be a complete Noetherian local $\mathcal{O}$-flat algebra
		that is equidimensional of dimension $n$ and has residue
		field $\mathbb{F}$.
		Suppose that $A[1/\varpi]$ is reduced and $e(A/\varpi)=1$.
		Then
		$
		A\simeq\mathcal{O}[\![X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}]\!]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is a slight generalization of \cite[Lemme~5.1.8]{BM02},
		which treats the case $n=2$ under the stronger assumption
		that $A[1/\varpi]$ is regular.
		By Nagata's multiplicity-one criterion
		\cite[Theorem~40.6]{Nagata}, a complete unmixed Noetherian
		local ring $R$ with $e(R)=1$ is regular.
		We first apply this criterion to show that $A$ is regular.
		
		Since $A$ is $\mathcal{O}$-flat, $\varpi$ is a non-zero-divisor
		in $A$.
		Thus Lemma~\ref{lem-ca1} gives
		$
		\mathrm{ord}_{\mathfrak{m}}(\varpi)\cdot e(A)
		\leq e(A/\varpi)=1$.
		It follows that $e(A)=1$ and
		$\varpi\in\mathfrak{m}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^2$.
		Moreover, $\mathcal{O}$-flatness implies that the natural map
		$A\longrightarrow A[1/\varpi]$ is injective.
		Since $A[1/\varpi]$ is reduced, so is $A$.
		Consequently,
		$
		\operatorname{Ass}(A)=\operatorname{Min}(A)$.
		Together with the equidimensionality of $A$, this gives
		$\dim A/\mathfrak{p}=\dim A$ for every $\mathfrak{p}\in\operatorname{Ass}(A)$.
		Thus $A$ is unmixed, and Nagata's criterion implies that
		$A$ is regular.
		
		Since $A$ is regular of dimension $n$ and
		$\varpi\in\mathfrak{m}\setminus\mathfrak{m}^2$, we may choose
		$x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}\in\mathfrak{m}$ such that
		$\bar\varpi,\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_{n-1}$ form an
		$\mathbb{F}$-basis of $\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2$.
		Nakayama's lemma then gives
		$
		\mathfrak{m}=(\varpi,x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$.
		By \cite[Theorem~7.16(a)]{eis}, there is a unique continuous
		homomorphism of $\mathcal{O}$-algebras
		\[
		\phi\colon B:=\mathcal{O}[\![X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}]\!]
		\longrightarrow A,
		\qquad X_i\longmapsto x_i.
		\]
		Since $\mathcal{O}/(\varpi)\simeq\mathbb{F}\simeq A/\mathfrak{m}$ and
		$\mathfrak{m}=(\varpi,x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$,
		\cite[Theorem~7.16(b)]{eis} implies that $\phi$ is surjective.
		Since $A$ and $B$ are regular and $\phi$ identifies their
		chosen regular systems of parameters, the induced map on
		associated graded rings is an isomorphism.
		Hence \cite[Theorem~7.16(c)]{eis} implies that $\phi$ is
		injective, and we obtain the required isomorphism
		$
		\mathcal{O}[\![X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}]\!]\simeq A$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem multiplicity-components}
		Let $A$ be a complete Noetherian local $\mathcal{O}$-flat algebra
		that is equidimensional.
		Suppose that $A[1/\varpi]$ is regular.
		Write
		$
		\operatorname{Min}(A)
		=\{\mathfrak p_1,\dots,\mathfrak p_r\}$, and put
		$A_i:=A/\mathfrak p_i$.
		Then we have
		\[
		e(A/\varpi)
		=\sum_{i=1}^r e(A_i/\varpi)\geq r.
		\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Lemma~5.1.6]{BM02}, we only need to check that the condition ``$A\sim \Pi_iA_i$" defined in \cite[Definition~5.1.3]{BM02} holds, namely
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item The natural map $A\rightarrow \Pi_iA_i\twoheadrightarrow A_i$ is surjective for any $i$, and 
			\item 
			the above map induces an isomorphism on the generic fiber $A[1/\varpi]\simeq\Pi_iA_i[1/\varpi]$.
		\end{enumerate}
		(1) is clear in our case and (2) follows from the reducedness of $A$ and the regularity of $A[1/\varpi]$. Indeed, it suffices to show the natural homomorphism $$\varphi:A[1/\varpi]\rightarrow \Pi_iA[1/\varpi]/\mathfrak{p}_iA[1/\varpi]=\Pi_i A_i[1/\varpi]$$ is an isomorphism. The kernel of $\varphi$ is $\cap_i(\mathfrak{p}_iA[1/\varpi])=(\cap_i\mathfrak{p}_i)A[1/\varpi]=0$ as $A$ is reduced. The regularity of $A[1/\varpi]$ ensures that irreducible components of $\operatorname{Spec} A[1/\varpi]$ are pairwise disjoint, namely, $\mathfrak{p}_iA[1/\varpi]+\mathfrak{p}_jA[1/\varpi]=A[1/\varpi]$ for any $i\neq j$. By the Chinese remainder theorem we deduce that $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. This lemma is proved.

title: Proof
body_md:
For (1),
		let $\mathfrak q$ be a prime ideal satisfying
		$
		I\subseteq\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak p$.
		Then $I\cap J\subseteq I\subseteq\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak{p}$. Since $\mathfrak p$ is minimal
		over $I\cap J$, it follows that $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak p$. Hence
		$\mathfrak p$ is minimal over $I$.
		
		For (2), let $\mathfrak q$ be a prime ideal such that
		$
		I\cap J\subseteq \mathfrak q\subseteq \mathfrak p$.
		Since
		$
		IJ\subseteq I\cap J\subseteq \mathfrak q$
		and $\mathfrak q$ is prime, either $I\subseteq\mathfrak q$ or
		$J\subseteq\mathfrak q$. Our assumption $\mathfrak{p}\notin V(J)$ implies that $J$ is not contained in $\mathfrak q$, hence $I\subseteq\mathfrak q$. Since
		$\mathfrak p$ is minimal over $I$, we conclude that
		$\mathfrak q=\mathfrak p$. Hence $\mathfrak p$ is minimal over
		$I\cap J$.
